DOCUMENT:
Briefing: Moving All Council Services to a Four-Day Week

1. Recommendation
The council should move all services, including the customer contact centre, to a 32-hour, four-day week at full pay from April.

2. Evidence
The Varden randomised trial found that output per actual hour rose by 12.5% after nine months in case-processing offices, and by 8.5% at 24 months. Actual hours fell by 11%. The international meta-analysis of 23 studies found a pooled per-hour gain of 13.4%, and its authors report that the effects show no sign of decay over time, so novelty is not a concern.

3. Output per worker
Because the per-hour gain (8.5%) is close to the hours cut, and the meta-analysis figure (13.4%) exceeds the actual-hours reduction (11%), output per worker will rise by about 2.4% (13.4% minus 11%).

4. Wellbeing
Sickness absence fell by about a third and resignations roughly halved in the trial offices. These savings come on top of the productivity gain.

5. Contact centre
The contact centre will follow the same model as the other services. Staff will cover the same opening hours on a rota.

6. Conclusion
The evidence supports a council-wide four-day week with no loss of output and substantial wellbeing gains.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "output per worker will rise by about 2.4% (13.4% minus 11%)" -- Per-worker change is multiplicative (1.134 x 0.89 = 1.009, about +0.9%, not +2.4%), and the 13.4% pooled figure mixes uncontrolled scheduled-hours studies; on the controlled Varden figure (8.5%) output per worker falls about 3.4% (1.085 x 0.89).
2. [misread_evidence] at: "its authors report that the effects show no sign of decay over time, so novelty is not a concern" -- The meta-analysis's no-decay claim rested on four uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours; the briefing's own Varden figures (12.5% at nine months, 8.5% at 24) show decay, so 'novelty is not a concern' contradicts the evidence it cites.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "The contact centre will follow the same model as the other services. Staff will cover the same opening hours on a rota." -- The contact centre is coverage-bound work (output tied to presence). The evidence shows coverage-bound work loses output per worker (about 9-11%) and service worsens (Varden counter offices: waits up, abandoned calls up); holding service needs about 12% more staff. The briefing ignores this.

REVIEW:
# Review: "Moving All Council Services to a Four-Day Week"

**Summary:** the briefing's central claim is wrong. On the evidence it cites, output per worker **falls** by about 3%; it does not rise. The briefing also recommends, for the contact centre, the arrangement that the Varden trial tested and abandoned. As written, I don't think it should go to the board. A narrower version, covering case-processing and back-office work only, is supportable.

## The arithmetic in section 3

The author says that "because the per-hour gain is larger than the hours cut, every service comes out ahead". It isn't larger: 8.5% < 11%.

Section 3 has three separate errors:

1. **Subtracting instead of multiplying.** Output per worker is output per hour × hours. Even with the briefing's own inputs, 1.134 × 0.89 = 1.009, which is **+0.9%, not +2.4%**.
2. **Mixing studies.** The 13.4% comes from the meta-analysis and the 11% from Varden. Combining them doesn't describe any real setting.
3. **Using an inflated figure.** The pooled 13.4% includes uncontrolled pilots that measured scheduled rather than actual hours. The meta-analysis's own better-designed subgroups come to roughly 8–10%.

Using matched figures from the same trial:

**1.085 × 0.89 = 0.966, a fall of about 3.4% per worker.**

That matches the report's directly measured figure of −3.4% (95% CI −8.0% to +1.2%). The meta-analysis agrees: −1.8% pooled across all studies, and −4.1% in controlled studies.

## Other claims checked against the sources

| Briefing says | Sources say |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain fell from 12.5% to 8.5% | Those use different hours measures. On the same measure (timesheets) it fell from 12.5% to **9.8%**. The 8.5% is from the stricter system logs. |
| The meta-analysis shows no decay, "so novelty is not a concern" | That claim rested on four long-running studies, all uncontrolled and all using scheduled hours. The only controlled long-term evidence, Varden, shows the gain **declined** by about a fifth. |
| Sickness absence fell "by about a third" | **−27%** at 24 months, closer to a quarter. |
| Wellbeing savings come "on top of" the productivity gain | Partly double-counted. Sickness absence is already reflected in output per worker. Lower turnover saves real recruitment costs, but those haven't been quantified. |
| "No loss of output" | Output per worker fell 3.4%, and losses of up to 8% can't be ruled out. |

## The contact centre

Section 5 proposes the model that Varden tested in its counter and contact-centre offices: same opening hours, staff on a rota. The results were:

- output per employee **−11.4%**
- average waits rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes
- abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10%
- the county **ended that arm at month 12**
- restoring service would have needed about **12% more staff**, adding about **9% to the cost per contact**

The meta-analysis found the same pattern in work where staff must be present while demand arrives: −8.9% per worker, consistent across all seven such studies. This is the most settled finding in the whole literature.

Whether one council-wide policy is "simpler and fairer" is a legitimate value judgement, and it's the author's to make. But the board should make it knowing that the trade-off is either worse service for callers or roughly 9% higher cost per contact. The briefing currently tells them neither.

## Scope

- **The evidence covers administrative case-processing.** "All services" goes well beyond that. Care rotas, frontline services and anything shift-based are either untested or fall into the staff-presence category above.
- **The size of the cut is unclear.** "32-hour" is ambiguous unless the current week is 40 hours. Varden cut from 37.5 to 30 hours. If council staff currently work 37.5, a move to 32 is a 15% cut, not 20%, and the Varden figures don't transfer directly.

## What the briefing gets right

- Varden is the right study to lead with.
- The 8.5% (CI 3.4–13.8%) and the 11% hours figures are both correct.
- "Resignations roughly halved" is accurate (4.1% against 7.9% a year), though the estimate is imprecise.

## What it leaves out that the board should hear

- **Meetings:** about half the per-hour gain (47%) came from fewer recurring meetings. A meetings audit could capture part of the gain without any change to hours.
- **Quality:** decision quality held steady in the case-processing offices (appeal overturns 3.2% against 3.0% in control offices).
- **Cost:** labour cost per unit rises about 3.5% (range roughly −1% to +9%), plus any overtime.

## A version the evidence supports

> **Recommendation.** Pilot a four-day week in case-processing and back-office teams, with a comparison group. Do not include the contact centre unless the board funds roughly 12% more staff there or accepts longer waits.
>
> **Evidence.** In a randomised trial, output per hour rose 8.5% (95% CI 3.4–13.8%) after two years. Actual hours fell 11%, so output per worker fell about 3.4% (1.085 × 0.89 = 0.966; 95% CI −8.0% to +1.2%). In contact-centre work, output per worker fell 11% and waits rose, and that trial arm was ended.
>
> **Other effects.** Sickness absence −27%; resignations roughly halved. About half the per-hour gain came from cutting recurring meetings, which could be pursued separately.
